abbey_verger.text: Welcome to Westminster Abbey. Voices low, boots soft, and no running on the royal tombs.
Kings and queens have been crowned here since 1066. William the Conqueror was first, on Christmas Day.
The Abbey is a Royal Peculiar. It answers to the monarch, not to a bishop. Quite the dress code.
The old Coronation Chair is covered in carved scribbles by schoolboys and visitors from hundreds of years ago. Please do not add yours.

abbey_visitor.text: I am looking for Poets' Corner. Geoffrey Chaucer was buried here in 1400, and the poets followed him. A very good neighbourhood.

then.text: My little tour sheet is the most borrowed thing in the Abbey after the umbrellas. Thank you.
Three more for your own corner: Burns is in Dumfries, Dylan Thomas has a stone here but his heart is in Laugharne, and Heaney never had a plaque here at all. He is at Bellaghy, with his own people.
Wordsworth, Shakespeare and Austen. All three. Austen has only had a memorial here since 1967, and she had to be very dead and very famous to get it.
Here, the first copy of the tour sheet, and a little anthology from the shop. Short poems. The Abbey prefers it if people finish things.

else.text: Wordsworth and Shakespeare, lovely. Jane Austen is the last: a blue plaque on Sydney Place in Bath, where she lived from 1801. Read it for me.
Still two to go. Shakespeare has a board inside the Globe across the river, and Austen a plaque in Bath. The Abbey is patient. It has had the practice.
The Lakes first, if you would. There is a lectern by the water in the Lake District about the daffodils. Wordsworth would have walked it. You can take the train.
{greeting} Welcome to Poets' Corner. Chaucer was buried here in 1400, Spenser in 1599, and then everybody wanted the neighbours.
I am writing a one-page tour sheet, 'Three Poets, Three Places', and I need someone to go and read the plaques where the poets actually lived, so I get the wording right.
Wordsworth's daffodils in the Lake District, Shakespeare at the Globe, and Jane Austen in Bath. Read all three and come back. The Abbey can offer tea and a small book. Mostly tea.
